speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I noted in my speech then that terrestrial and online gambling are two very different realms that would require different approaches to address the problems associated with gambling in general.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I would like to refer to a section of the speech made by the then Minister for Social and Family Development, Mr Chan Chun Sing, on online gambling, and I quote: "This is an evolving challenge.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We need to stay vigilant to stay ahead of the threat and the challenges.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We need to stay ahead and be prepared to strengthen our safeguards as necessary proactively and creatively.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And we need concerted efforts by all – individuals, family and society – to keep our eyes on this issue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And we need to make sure that our measures are multi-pronged – upstream, midstream and downstream." During the last session of Parliament, I directed some supplementary questions at the current Minister for Social and Family Development about these multi-pronged measures that the Government had sought to introduce to check online gambling.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Why do I call online gambling a scourge?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The American Psychiatric Association places pathological gambling in the same category as drug dependency and alcoholism in its Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It says that gambling "activate(s) the brain reward system with effects similar to those of drugs of abuse" and that "gambling disorder symptoms resemble substance use disorders to a certain extent." Numerous academic studies have found that online gambling is more addictive than other types of gambling and that online gamblers have higher rates of gambling addiction than traditional gamblers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Internet has greatly increased the accessibility of gambling.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The problem was found to be especially serious among young people – online gambling has become the main form of pathological gambling among people below 26 years old in Spain.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These results are unsurprising, since Millennials are more comfortable using Internet technologies than their older counterparts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Problem and pathological gamblers can place bets using their smart phones without their friends and family members even noticing, unlike when they visit the casinos or go to the Turf Club.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This removes a very important informal safeguard against problem gambling.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: An important part of addiction treatment is for the problem gambler to avoid putting himself in situations which could tempt him to lapse back to his bad habit, for example, by avoiding casinos, jackpot rooms or other physical locations where gambling is available.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, it would be impractical to expect a problem gambler to refrain from using his mobile phone or computer as these are needed for modern day work and personal communication.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A longitudinal study of gambling and problem gambling in the US between 1999 and 2013 found that problem gambling affects the poor more than the rich.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The prevalence of frequent gambling is highest in the poorest one-third of respondents and those in disadvantaged neighbourhoods, and it declines dramatically as socio-economic status increases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This could be because some in the lower-income group are motivated to gamble so as to improve their financial situation and status.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The most common reaction I have heard from Singaporeans to the news of the issuing of exempt operator licences is that the Government just wants to "make more money".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While I am sure the Minister will refute this accusation vigorously, the fact remains that a large part of legalised gambling revenue goes into the state's coffers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is providing for exempt operators a way to redirect gambling spending away from illegal overseas operators to local operators, which are owned by the Tote Board?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If so, this only fuels public speculation that the Government simply wants a piece of the huge global Internet gambling pie and that this is a revenue-raising exercise done at the expense of Singaporeans and their welfare.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some have argued that the Tote Board gives money to many charities which help the vulnerable in our society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is a morally questionable argument that is akin to saying that it is okay to harm some people in order to help others.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister said that the Government looked at similar exempt operator regimes in Hong Kong and Norway and found that the problem gambling situation did not worsen.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am not sure what these studies or what the exact findings were.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Minister will be able to share the details of these studies for Singaporeans to examine.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Did these studies prove that having an exempt operator regime reduces gambling harm more than a complete prohibition of online gambling?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If not, was the Government too eager to rush to exempt operators before more conclusive results are found?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the aftermath of the National Council of Churches of Singapore's (NCCS's) dialogue with the Government, it was reported the carve-out created for exempt operators to legally provide online gambling facilities was based on studies relating to the social impact of gambling that the Government had documented, and its assessment of possible scenarios with and without the "valve" of controlled exempt operator.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: NCCS noted that the research on this area is still new.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this extent at the very least, the Government should publish its research in this area, especially since the Government will reportedly be meeting up with NCCS leaders in three to six months' time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister has argued that exempt operators provide an "outlet" for gamblers and allow the Government to manage crime associated with gambling.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The assumption behind this argument is that gamblers who were gambling on illegal overseas gambling websites will switch over to the exempt operators' websites or apps.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Has the Government found any studies to show that people will actually switch over to exempt operators?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More likely, local gambling apps that have a stamp of approval by the Government will attract people who have previously never gambled online.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It may include many young people who may not relish queuing up at Toto outlets or going to the races at the Turf Club but may experiment with gambling for the first time from the privacy of their phones.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The legalisation of online gambling will thus expand the gambling market, rather than provide a safe outlet for existing gamblers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Once started, online gambling, like soft drugs, could be a gateway to more serious gambling addictions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In its meeting with NCCS, it was reported that the Government told NCCS that it was not sending conflicting signals with the partial lifting of the ban on online gambling because the exemptions had already been written into the Bill in 2014.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would appear these exemptions were written specifically with Singapore Pools and Singapore Turf Club in mind.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A quick review of the timeline of events is as follows: October 2014: Remote Gambling Bill passed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: July 2015: Singapore Pools and Singapore Turf Club (STC) applied for exemptions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the eyes of the public, it would seem that the year-long evaluation of the applications was conducted with one outcome in mind – to find a way for Singapore Pools and the Turf Club to carry out online gambling operations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Was the process meant to determine whether or not the applications should be approved, or to determine how they could be approved?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: During the 2014 debate, I asked the Minister to put the Bill before a Select Committee so as to scrutinise the exemption clauses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This request was turned down as the House was told that the Government had already engaged in consultations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, in its recent meeting with NCCS, the Government cited its consultations with social service leaders and religious representatives as justification for the exemptions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Was NCCS part of the "religious representatives" consulted in drafting the Bill?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If so, why have they changed their position and, if not, why were they not consulted before?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While feedback through the Government channels, any Government channel, should not be discouraged and, in fact, encouraged, we should remember that they are not subject to the same degree of Parliamentary scrutiny in terms of the range of opinions consulted and the extent of public scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On Bills that provoke as much controversy as this one, should we not take the extra step to establish relevant Select Committees to go over the implementation and provisions with a fine-tooth comb?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In exchange for a bit more time, we gain the opportunity to deepen public engagement and generate greater support for our laws.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government says that there are safeguards in place to prevent gambling addicts from harming themselves and their families.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, self-exclusion is only practical for those who recognise that they have a problem.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As for third party exclusion, a family member has to cross several difficult hurdles to get his or her loved one placed on the exclusion list.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This includes being interviewed by a panel and having to show proof of the family member's gambling addiction.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The surreptitious nature of online gambling addiction means that such proof will be hard to obtain.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Also, most problem gamblers do not seek help until they hit rock bottom, for example, if they have wiped out all their family savings.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These suggest that the numbers affected by problem gambling are much higher than official statistics may show.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Unlike other vices like alcoholism and drug abuse, the costs associated with problem gambling are borne almost entirely by family members, who often end up paying off the debts of the gambler.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The embarrassment associated with problem gambling means that the gamblers and their families rarely talk about their problems in public.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Because of this, there is a tendency for policymakers to overlook the real social impact of problem gambling.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Anecdotally, many cases of loan sparking "runners" are linked to problem gambling.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There should be better statistics gathered on such tragedies to better establish the extent of their links to problem gambling.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This will enable a proper assessment of the impact of the exemptions on the rates of gambling and problem gambling.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We need to look further downstream to prevent gambling habits from taking root.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would appear that many young men are introduced to the habit during their National Service days through army mates, or at their workplaces.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More targeted public education is needed, especially among young people, if we are to prevent the scourge of gambling, especially online gambling, from spreading in our society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The best safeguard is to lessen the avenues for Singaporeans to get introduced to gambling.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To conclude, Mdm Speaker, there has been a glaring lack of clarity as to how the Government is making preparations to address the scourge of online gambling downstream, midstream and upstream in a directed and committed way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is in spite of the Government's open admission that online gambling is, I quote, a "difficult challenge".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would logically follow that the issue would demand significant attention from the authorities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, one cannot help but get the feeling that it is business as usual, and that online gambling is just another game to gamble on, or just another sport for the public to take a bet on.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am concerned that it is much more ominous than that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Member has raised numerous questions and made rather serious allegations about motivations of the Government, whether it consulted certain parties, whether this is the Government trivialising the risks posed to Singaporeans by online gambling.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: All in all, I am rather disturbed by the picture the Member has painted, notwithstanding all that we have put up, public statements and all the things that the Government has put in place to tackle precisely what he has said about the scourge of gambling and scourge of online gambling.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is by no means an unimportant task.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Member is calling for transparency, but I think it is better suited to written replies to Parliamentary Questions, which the Member can file.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In fact, I understand that Mr Leon Perera had filed some questions about the experience in both Hong Kong and Norway, which were meant for today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And in the interest of ensuring that everything comes out today, if the Member is prepared to allow it to come out, we have a comprehensive reply for him.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I propose we use the remaining time to keep our eyes focused on the big picture, precisely what the Member is concerned about.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Both the Government and the Opposition agree that online gambling addiction poses serious concerns that we are all concerned about, notwithstanding the Member's assertion that the Government is completely unconcerned and is trying to make money out of this; the most disturbing thing I have heard this evening.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Members from across the aisle have also spoken about the harm.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I think Members like Ms Denise Phua would be very concerned if the impression is given that she and other Members are not concerned.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: From a law and order perspective, illegal online gambling has links and associations with syndicates and organised crime, including transnational organised crime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In November 2015, the South China Morning Post reported that Chinese police had busted a multinational online gambling syndicate which allegedly generated more than US$78 billion in bets and served nearly a million registered members in China alone.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Let us run through some of the key points again, as we had raised them previously.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And if this carries on, it will double in a matter of years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: With Singapore's high Internet and smartphone penetration rate and tech savvy population, I do not think we will be spared from this global trend.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I think the Member would have heard this data last month.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: After the Remote Gambling Act was brought into force, Singapore now has one of the most extensive and proactive set of measures in the world against online gambling – blocking of sites, blocking payments, blocking advertisements, criminalising users who go onto online websites.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Yet, as the Member also accepts, in 2014, with virtual private network (VPN) and other technology, with new sites popping up every day, illicit online gambling still exists in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I mentioned the South China Morning Post report.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: That syndicate is alleged to have operated more than 500 sites at the point of investigation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Ministry of Home Affairs continues to see Internet traffic from Singapore to blocked sites and new sites.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Police have observed the trend over recent years of organised crime syndicates in Singapore moving from the terrestrial gambling sphere to online gambling.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And arrests continue to be made for illegal gambling, both syndicates and punters alike.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And more than one-third of those arrested for illegal lotteries were involved in online remote lotteries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, I do not think the Member is right to suggest that we are unaware of the risks of online gambling.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In fact, all that has been in place since 2014 is to deal with this scourge of online gambling that envelopes the work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To make things worse, online gambling sites are attracting younger Singaporeans, as the Member also accepts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: A study prior to the passage of the Remote Gambling Act found that about two-thirds of respondents who had participated in remote gambling were between 25 and 44 years old.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our assessment, Madam, is that this problem will still grow in Singapore and a total ban on its own will not be sufficient to deal with this problem, however much we may believe that to be so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, we do need to ask Mr Singh and his colleagues from the Workers' Party: do you accept that the global trend of illicit online gambling is growing worldwide?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Do you accept that given how open and wired Singapore is, we will not be spared from the problem?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Do you accept that, even with extensive blocking systems as is the case now, illicit online gambling is still present in Singapore, and the problem can still grow?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: If the answer is "yes", and I am not sure what the Member's answer will be, then the question is what the solution ought to be.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: What has been the Workers' Party's proposals on the online gambling problem thus far?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In 2014, during the Second Reading of the Remote Gambling Bill, many Members of the Workers' Party in this House spoke and opposed the exemption regime but did not offer many details of alternative solutions to eradicate social ills caused by online gambling.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Yee Jenn Jong made suggestions on how the exempt operator regime could be tightened if it was implemented.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In the 2015 manifesto, the Workers' Party had one line or a couple of lines on online gambling – prohibit all online gambling; no exceptions, and its aim was, I quote, "to eradicate the social ills caused by online and remote gambling".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we presume, in 2015, the Workers' Party's objective and proposal to Singaporeans was to drive online gambling in Singapore to zero, through a total ban.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In its 27 September 2016 press release, the Workers' Party opposed the granting of exemption to any organisation but did not offer a solution to eradicate the social ills caused by online gambling.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: No need for a valve with social safeguards.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We should not put it to good use.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We should not get involved in having any safety valves, any social safeguards.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But, Madam, their position is not clear for a number of reasons which I shall submit.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, they do not cite any precedent or any country in the world where a complete ban has solved this growing problem of online gambling addiction.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, they do not explain why Singapore's approach, and those, such as in Norway and Hong Kong, which have adapted from our system, and which have valves, are inferior.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Even after this evening, even after the allegations have been made about the Government's intentions, I do not think we are any wiser.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Singh's explanation, Madam, is that, with a total ban, most gamblers, he says, would just go to the existing land-based outlets, such as authorised 4-D or Toto shops, which are completely legal and regulated.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But this is not the view of the professionals, the Police, who have seen the problem go underground and who say that this will happen, and it is happening.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, it is imperative, as Minister Iswaran has said in 2014, for Mr Singh making these assertions, flying in the face of what the Police, the professionals, have observed and said it is happening, to provide evidence instead that a total ban will not drive illegal activities underground but will instead drive it to the land-based Toto shops.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Fourth, apart from what we have just talked about, there are no details in their manifesto, media releases and speeches on how their proposal of a total and complete ban will solve this real problem inflicted on many Singaporeans, some of whom we have met at Meet-the-People Sessions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And this after two years of debate since the Act was enacted in 2014.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, we invite the Workers' Party to make clear what its position is.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Is it an objection in principle, against all gambling?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If it is a matter of principle, then state that it is so, both land and terrestrial.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But if it is against online gambling, then it is an assessment of where the risks lie.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And as I have said earlier, we have the views of the Police and the professionals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In such a case, it would be good if the Workers' Party can put on the table specific suggestions on how it would enact a total ban to solve the problem and make it drive the problem from online to the land-based terrestrial outlets that Mr Singh had categorically said in 2014.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, does Mr Singh support a complete ban on VPN and technology that skirts around blocking measures?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, we know, Madam, that law, as a deterrence, is not just about the law and deterrence, but the likelihood of getting caught.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Are they proposing to have apps or tracking devices uploaded on computers or smartphones to monitor people and further detect that they are going onto illicit sites and, perhaps, after that, do you propose to make it mandatory for counselling?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Or are you proposing to increase penalties and up prosecution rates and to ask for deterrent sentences?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: How will you make the prohibition and the enforcement of the prohibition, such as to promote the flow of people from the illicit sites online to the Toto and Singapore Pool sites on land?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Or are you proposing to expand outreach and education and mandatory counselling and, if so, do you believe that it will solve the problem?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It may not always be popular but we have to try to solve the problem pragmatically and, most importantly, be prepared to adjust our solution along the way, based on experience and our findings.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is right here on our shores, in our homes, in people's pockets when they walk around, when they work, when they are at home.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It poses law and order and social problems, like I said before.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And online gambling is associated with syndicates and organised crime.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Senior Minister of State Lee, you have to conclude.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For those of us in this House and outside who have moral objections to gambling, including some of us who are speaking, do not visit, discourage your friends and family, and help the National Council on Problem Gambling and voluntary welfare organisations who work hard day after day to tackle these social aspects and the scourge of the problem.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Please end your speech, Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: The time allowed for the proceedings has expired.
